L7@P0: Abstract
L8@P0: In his Ph.D. thesis, Ira Gessel proved a reciprocity formula for noncommutative
L9@P0: symmetric functions which enables one to count words and permutations with restrictions on the lengths of their increasing runs. We generalize Gessel’s theorem to allow
L10@P0: for a much wider variety of restrictions on increasing run lengths, and use it to complete
L11@P0: the enumeration of permutations with parity restrictions on peaks and valleys, and to
L12@P0: give a systematic method for obtaining generating functions for permutation statistics
L13@P0: that are expressible in terms of increasing runs. Our methods can also be used to obtain
L14@P0: analogous results for alternating runs in permutations.
L15@P0: Keywords: permutations, increasing runs, peaks, valleys, noncommutative symmetric functions
L16@P0: 1. Introduction
L17@P0: Given a set A, let A∗ be the set of all finite sequences of elements of A, including the empty
L18@P0: sequence. We call A an alphabet, the elements of A letters, A∗the free monoid on A,

L20@P0: the elements of A∗ words. If we refer to words without specifying an alphabet, then we take
L21@P0: the alphabet to be P, the set of positive integers. Suppose that our alphabet A is a totally
L22@P0: ordered set, such as P. Then every word in A∗can be uniquely decomposed into a sequence
L23@P0: of maximal weakly increasing consecutive subsequences, which we call increasing runs. For
L24@P0: example, the increasing runs of 2142353 are 2, 14, 235, and 3. The notion of increasing runs
L25@P0: clearly extends to permutations as well.

L27@P0: functions for words and permutations with restrictions on the lengths of their increasing runs.

L29@P0: run theorem that will enable us to count words and permutations with an even wider variety

L147@P2: 2. The run theorem
L148@P2: 2.1. Basic definitions
L149@P2: Here we give the definitions for some of the basic concepts of this paper, including descent
L150@P2: compositions and noncommutative symmetric functions.
L151@P2: Given a permutation π in Sn, we say that i ∈ [n − 1] is a descent of π if πi > πi+1.
L152@P2: Then, increasing runs of π can be characterized as maximal consecutive subsequences of π
L153@P2: containing no descents. Let us call an increasing run short if it has length 1, and long if it
L154@P2: has length at least 2.
L155@P2: The number of increasing runs of a nonempty permutation is one more than its number
L156@P2: of descents; in fact, the lengths of the increasing runs determine the descents, and vice versa.
L157@P2: Given a subset S ⊆ [n − 1] with elements s1 < s2 < · · · < sj, let C(S) be the composition
L158@P2: (s1, s2 − s1, . . . , sj − sj−1, n − sj ) of n, and given a composition L = (L1, L2, . . . , Lk), let
L159@P2: D(L) = {L1, L1 + L2, . . . , L1 + · · · + Lk−1} be the corresponding subset of [n − 1]. Then,
L160@P2: C and D are inverse bijections. If π is a permutation with descent set S, we call C(S) the
L161@P2: descent composition of π, which give the lengths of the increasing runs of π. Applying D to
L162@P2: the descent composition of a permutation gives its descent set.
L163@P2: The definitions and properties of descents, increasing runs, and descent compositions
L164@P2: extend naturally to words in the free monoid on any totally ordered alphabet such as [n] or
L165@P2: P. Note that increasing runs in words are allowed to be weakly increasing, whereas increasing
L166@P2: runs in permutations are necessarily strictly increasing since no letters repeat.

L4: # Ira M. Gessel and Yan Zhuang
L5: # Homomorphisms on noncommutative symmetric functions and permutation enumeration
L6: Abstract. We present a unifying framework for deriving permutation enumeration formulas involving restrictions on descent compositions or permutation statistics describable in terms of descent compositions: these formulas can be proven by first lifting them to the algebra of noncommutative symmetric functions and then applying an appropriate homomorphism. We give several applications of this method including rederivations and extensions of classical results in the literature as well as new results.
